title: Simultaneous and total-sum constraints
transcript: Simultaneous conditions describe the same unknowns at the same time. A solution must make every condition true together. Put a label on each unknown before you use a symbol. As you work, keep the same label attached to the same quantity.

In AMC Upper Primary practice, look for two totals or a sum and a difference describing the same values. A diagram or short equation can collect the clues in one place. In a Rossmoyne style puzzle, two or more conditions can constrain the same value. Substitute your result into the original conditions to prove it fits.
Two numbers add to twenty. The larger is four more than the smaller. What are they? Picture the two amounts lined up, with an extra piece on the larger one.
Remove the extra four from the total. The remaining sixteen comprises two equal copies of the smaller number. So the smaller is eight and the larger is twelve. Check both the sum and the difference.
Two notebooks and a ruler cost thirty dollars. One notebook and two rulers cost thirty-three dollars. Find the price of one notebook plus one ruler, then recover each price.

Add the equations, giving three notebooks and three rulers for sixty-three dollars. Divide by three. One of each costs twenty-one dollars. Subtract that from the price of two notebooks and a ruler. The notebook costs nine, leaving twelve for the ruler. Both original prices work.
Three boxes A, B and C contain counters. Boxes A and B together hold twenty-one. B and C hold twenty-six. C and A hold twenty-three. Find how many counters are in each box.

Add all three conditions. Each box appears twice, so the combined sum seventy is twice the number of counters in the three boxes. Halve it to get the complete total thirty-five. Subtract a pair's total to find the missing box. Subtract B plus C to get A equals nine. The same method gives B equals twelve and C equals fourteen.
The resulting pairs total twenty-one, twenty-six and twenty-three. Each matches its clue. The original clues forced the overall total and then each single box. There can be only one such assignment.
A single total can fit many pairs. Use the second condition to choose a particular pair. In the three pair totals, each single quantity appears twice. Divide the combined pair totals by two.

Name the unknown quantity and write what each given relationship says about it. Label your equations with the units used in the story. Recheck the result by applying the original relationships, including each bound, whole-number rule or shared total.
